newsitem.title: USA: Crime still biggest concern to New Yorkers - poll.
newsitem.headline: Crime still biggest concern to New Yorkers - poll.

text.p: New York City residents overwhelming agreed crime still is a "big problem," a survey said, even though 51 percent felt the city has gotten safer in the past three years.
By a 65 to 34 percent margin, New Yorkers said that being a victim of a crime was something they personally worry about.

"Perceptions about crime are complex: New Yorkers feel crime is more of a problem citywide than in their own neighborhoods, but almost two-thirds say they personally fear becoming a crime victim," said Maurice Carroll, director of the Quinnipiac College Polling Institute.

Although only 25 percent of the 845 residents surveyed by Quinnipiac College volunteered that crime was the most important problem facing the city, when asked specifically if they thought it was a problem, 81 percent called it a big problem.

Both Mayor Rudolph Giuliani and Police Commissioner Howard Safir got high ratings for their anti-crime efforts, with Giuliani's approval rating reaching 81 percent to 15 percent. Safir got a 55 to 17 percent approval rating for his performance.

Giuliani, whose election campaign hinges on the big drops in crime his Administration has achieved, said that for the first nine months of 1996 felony complaints in the seven categories fell by 36.2 percent when compared to the rates seen in the same period in 1993, in his September management report.
Reports of shooting victims fell 46.3 percent from January to June of 1996, when compared with the 1993 period.

But not all New Yorkers see big improvements, as 37 percent of those polled by Quinnipiac College from February 3 to 9 said the city was about as safe as it was three years ago, and 10 pecent said it was less safe.
And city residents want newly hired police officers to live in New York City by a 64 to 32 percent margin.
